title: Growing leek microgreens
subtitle: Slow-growing allium microgreens with a mild onion flavour, cut in 14 to 21 days
excerpt: Leek microgreens take two to three weeks from sowing to the cutting stage, longer than most brassica microgreens. The result is a grass-like shoot with a mild onion flavour, useful in salads, soups, and egg dishes.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Leek microgreens are a slow allium crop that takes 14 to 21 days from sowing to the cutting stage. Sow densely on a 25 cm tray, blackout for four to five days until the shoots emerge, then move to light for the remaining 10 to 16 days until the grass-like shoots are 10 to 12 cm tall. The flavour is mild onion, pleasant in salads, soups, and egg dishes.

The allium microgreens (leek, onion, chive) are slower than brassicas and require more patience, but the wait is straightforward. The tray needs light and bottom-watering for two weeks; the main risk is the extended damp period encouraging mould on the growing medium surface.

Light: a bright south-facing windowsill works in spring and summer. In the darker months a supplementary LED grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray, running 14 hours a day, is recommended. Leek microgreens in low light lean strongly toward the light source and produce thin, pale stems.
Temperature: 18 to 22°C. Allium microgreens are less cold-tolerant than brassicas. Below 16°C germination is slow and irregular; aim for a consistently warm room.

Day 0: sow. Pre-dampen seed compost and fill the tray to within 1 cm of the rim. Scatter leek microgreen seed at 20 to 30 g per 25 cm tray; leek seed is angular and black, easy to distribute evenly. Press gently into contact with the medium.

Days 1 to 5: blackout. Allium seeds take longer to germinate than brassicas; the blackout phase runs four to five days until the looped shoots straighten and push to 2 to 3 cm. Leek shoots emerge as a U-shaped loop (the seed coat still attached at the top) before straightening; this is normal. Remove the cover once the majority of shoots are standing upright.
Day 6 onward: light. Move to a bright position. Leek shoots green up more slowly than brassicas; allow 48 hours in good light before the full colour develops.

throughout the growing phase: set the tray inside a second tray with 1 to 2 cm of water each day and let the medium absorb it. Leek microgreens need consistent moisture over the extended growing period; do not allow the medium to dry out between waterings.

Days 14 to 21: cut. When shoots are 10 to 12 cm tall and standing upright, cut 1 cm above the medium surface with scissors. The shoots are hollow and slightly waxy. Rinse, use fresh or refrigerate for up to three days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems on leek microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Mould on the medium surface after day 7
items.cause: Extended damp period in a warm, still room.
items.fix: Increase airflow around the tray with a small fan at low speed. Bottom-water only; never top-water. The mould is on the substrate, not the shoots; the leek stems remain safe to cut.

items.symptom: Slow or failed germination after day 6
items.cause: Old seed, cold room, or medium too dry in the germination window.
items.fix: Leek seed viability declines after 2 to 3 years. Test seed in a damp cloth germination test before a full tray. Aim for room temperature above 18°C.

items.symptom: Thin, leaning stems that fall over
items.fix: Move to a brighter window or add a grow light. Leek microgreens lean strongly toward the light source; rotating the tray 180 degrees every two days produces more even growth.

items.symptom: Stems collapse and rot at base
items.fix: Bottom-water only and remove standing water from the outer tray after 30 minutes. Discard the affected tray and restart.

content.text: Leek seed viability drops more quickly than brassica seed; aim to use seed from the current or previous season. Standard vegetable leek seed is usually untreated (leek is grown by direct sowing and fungicide coatings are uncommon). Microgreen suppliers stock leek in packs sized for tray growing.
